per_pair.why: Rich isometric game environment with distinct enemy types and visual depth versus sparse dark background with minimal jellyfish creatures.
Five characterful, visually distinct enemy types (Husk, Ember Wisp, Brute, Mite) with clear personality versus four nearly identical simple jellyfish.
Dynamic attack animations with clear telegraph poses and varied enemy types versus stiff, mechanical attacks from identical creatures.
Explosive, screen-filling death effects with debris and impact versus simple linear death animations with no visual feedback.

loser_biggest_gap: Enemy design and visual characterization: Game A's minimal jellyfish enemies lack distinct identities, personalities, and visual interest compared to Game B's clearly differentiated types (ranged fire caster, melee brute, swarm mites, shambling tank).
loser_other_gaps: Animation feedback and impact: Game A's attacks and deaths have no particle effects, screen shake, or satisfying visual feedback—they feel weightless and mechanical.
Visual environment and polish: Game A exists in a dark void while Game B shows a cohesive, detailed isometric dungeon with lighting, depth, and environmental storytelling.
Attack telegraphing: Game A's animations are too simple to clearly telegraph what each enemy is doing; Game B's poses, timing, and effects make intent obvious at a glance.
reasoning: Game B decisively outperforms Game A across every criterion. Despite being more visually complex, it remains highly readable through isometric perspective and clear color coding. More critically, it has genuine character design—each enemy type has distinct silhouette, attack pattern, and personality. Game A's identical jellyfish creatures feel like placeholder art. Animation quality, death feedback, and environmental polish all clearly favor B. Game A reads as an early prototype while Game B feels like polished indie craft.
